title: Drawings That Move: Animation
summary: Long before computers, artists made drawings come alive by filming them one picture at a time. A dinosaur named Gertie bowed to her audience, a mouse whistled in perfect time with music, and a giant gorilla made of rabbit fur climbed a skyscraper. Here is how they did it.

sections.heading: Luminous Pantomimes at the Wax Museum
paragraphs: Imagine it is a chilly autumn evening in Paris on 28 October 1892. You push through the crowds at the Musée Grévin, a famous wax museum on the Boulevard Montmartre, and find your way into a small, dark room called the Cabinet Fantastique. A screen glows at the front. Then something astonishing happens: a painted clown named Pierrot strolls across the screen, sings a serenade under a window, and gets into a squabble with a rival. Nobody is wearing a costume. Nobody is on stage. The characters are paintings, and yet they move.

The man behind the screen was Émile Reynaud, the same French inventor you met earlier with his praxinoscope, the spinning toy with a ring of mirrors. Reynaud had kept tinkering. He wanted more than a ten-second loop that repeated forever. He wanted whole stories, with characters who walked in, did something funny, and walked off again. In 1888 he applied for a French patent on a machine he called the Théâtre Optique, the Optical Theatre, and the patent was granted in January 1889.

Here is how it worked. Reynaud painted every single picture by hand, in color, on small transparent squares of gelatin. He fastened hundreds of these squares one after another along a long flexible band, with holes along the edges so the band could be pulled smoothly over a wheel. Some bands were up to about 50 meters long. A lantern shone light through each little picture, and a clever arrangement of mirrors and lenses threw the moving characters onto the screen. A second lantern projected a painted background, such as a garden or a beach, so the characters seemed to move through a real place.

Reynaud did not use a motor. He cranked the band by hand, like a puppeteer, and he could speed up, slow down, or even run a gesture back and forth to stretch a moment for laughs. This meant a band of about 500 pictures could last around 12 to 15 minutes, far longer than you might expect. A musician played along, and at marked points on the band an electrical contact could set off a sound effect. Every show was a live performance, a little different each time.

Reynaud called his shows Pantomimes Lumineuses, or Luminous Pantomimes. The first program included Pauvre Pierrot (Poor Pierrot), made of about 500 images, Un bon bock (A Good Beer), with about 700, and Le Clown et ses chiens (The Clown and His Dogs). Later he added Autour d'une cabine (Around a Bathing Hut), a seaside comedy. The Grévin shows ran on and off until 1900, with more than 12,800 performances and over half a million visitors. That makes Reynaud's animated shows some of the very first projected moving pictures a paying audience ever saw, a few years before the Lumière brothers screened their photographic films just down the road.

Sadly, Reynaud's story has an unhappy ending. Hand-painting every frame was slow, and once photographic films arrived, audiences flocked to see real trains, real streets and real people. The Théâtre Optique could not compete. Around 1913, poor and discouraged, Reynaud is said to have smashed his last machine and thrown most of his picture bands into the River Seine. Only two of his bands survive today, including Pauvre Pierrot. In 2015 UNESCO added his Luminous Pantomimes to its Memory of the World Register, a list of the planet's most precious documents. Reynaud had shown that drawings could tell stories on a big screen. Others would now try to do it with a camera.

sections.heading: Chalk Faces, Dancing Lines and a Shy Dinosaur
paragraphs: A movie camera can be turned into an animation machine with a simple trick. Instead of filming a whole scene at once, you film just one frame, stop, change the drawing a tiny bit, then film one more frame. When the film is played back at normal speed, the tiny changes blur together into motion. Animators call this frame-by-frame or single-frame filming, and it is the same stop trick Georges Méliès used to make people vanish, applied one picture at a time.

One of the first people to use it for drawings was J. Stuart Blackton, a British-born American cartoonist who co-founded the Vitagraph film company in New York. In 1900 he had made The Enchanted Drawing, in which he sketched a face and objects that seemed to come alive. In 1906 Vitagraph released his Humorous Phases of Funny Faces, about three minutes long. Blackton draws faces in white chalk on a blackboard, and then the faces roll their eyes, puff smoke from a cigar, and change expression. Much of the film actually uses cutout paper pieces moved bit by bit, but in a few moments the drawings themselves change from frame to frame. Many historians call it the first animated cartoon recorded on standard movie film.

Across the Atlantic, a French caricaturist named Émile Cohl, then about 50 years old, was working for the Gaumont film company in Paris. On 17 August 1908 Gaumont released his Fantasmagorie. It lasts less than two minutes, but it took about 700 drawings. Cohl drew each one on paper with dark lines, filmed them, and printed the film as a negative, so the lines show up white on black, like chalk on a blackboard. In it, a little stick-figure clown is born from the artist's hand, and everything around him keeps transforming: a flower turns into a bottle, an elephant turns into a house, a man turns into a cannon. There is no real plot, just a joyful dream where anything can become anything else. That freedom, where a line can turn into whatever the artist imagines, is something only animation can do.

Then came Winsor McCay, an American newspaper cartoonist famous for his gorgeous comic strip Little Nemo in Slumberland. McCay was a speed-drawing star in vaudeville, the live variety shows of the time. In 1911 he animated his Little Nemo characters, and in 1912 he made How a Mosquito Operates, about a mosquito who drinks so much blood from a sleeping man that it pops. But his most famous creation premiered in February 1914: Gertie the Dinosaur.

McCay performed with Gertie live on stage. He stood beside the screen in a smart suit, holding a whip like a circus trainer, and called out commands. On the screen, an enormous, friendly brontosaurus peeked out from behind rocks, bowed, ate a tree, cried when she was scolded, and swallowed a whole lake. At the end, McCay walked behind the screen and appeared, drawn, riding away on Gertie's back. Audiences adored her because she had a personality. She was not just moving; she seemed to feel things, to be shy, playful and a bit naughty.

Making Gertie took enormous work. McCay and his assistant drew on thin, see-through mulberry paper so they could trace the background rocks and lake onto every sheet. McCay later boasted of 10,000 drawings, though historians think that number is probably exaggerated, because surviving copies contain only about seven minutes of animation. He also invented smart shortcuts. He drew the most important poses first, the key moments of an action, and then filled in the pictures between them. He used registration marks so each sheet lined up exactly, and he reused loops of drawings for repeated movements like Gertie's breathing. About 400 of the original Gertie drawings still survive, and in 1991 the US Library of Congress added the film to its National Film Registry.
McCay did not patent his methods. He thought of animation as an art. But not everyone saw it that way, and a new idea was about to turn cartoons into an industry.

sections.heading: The Clear-Sheet Sandwich: How Cel Animation Works
paragraphs: Think about the problem McCay faced. If Gertie stands in front of a rocky lake, and you need 24 pictures for every second she moves, then drawing the whole picture again and again means drawing those same rocks and that same lake thousands of times. It is exhausting, and the background wobbles a little in every copy, so it seems to shiver on screen.

The solution came from a young American animator named Earl Hurd, who in 1914 patented the idea of drawing the moving characters on clear sheets of celluloid, the same kind of transparent plastic used for film. These sheets became known as cels, short for celluloid. You paint the background just once, on paper or board. Then you lay a cel with the character on top. Wherever the cel is clear, the background shows through. Wherever the character is painted, it covers the background. For the next frame, you lift off that cel and lay down the next one, with the character in a slightly different pose. The background never has to be redrawn.

Cel animation turned cartoons into a team sport. Here is roughly how a big studio did it by the 1930s. A lead animator drew the key poses, the most important moments, such as a character's foot leaving the ground and landing again. Assistants called inbetweeners drew the pictures in between, so the motion flowed smoothly. Every sheet of paper had holes punched at the bottom that fit onto pegs on the drawing desk and under the camera, which kept every picture lined up perfectly. Then the drawings went to the ink and paint department. Inkers traced each outline carefully onto the front of a cel with pen or brush, and painters filled in the colors on the back of the cel, so the brushstrokes did not show from the front. At Disney, this delicate work was done mostly by women, many of whom were highly skilled artists whose names were rarely in the credits.

How many pictures are needed? Sound films ran at 24 frames per second. Animating on ones means drawing a new picture for every single frame, 24 drawings per second, which looks extra smooth and is used for fast or delicate action. Most of the time, animators worked on twos: each drawing is photographed for two frames in a row, so only 12 drawings are needed for each second. Your eye still sees smooth motion, and the studio saves half the work. A feature-length cartoon could still need well over 100,000 painted cels.

sections.heading: A Cat, a Rabbit and a Whistling Mouse
paragraphs: By the 1920s, cartoons were a regular part of a trip to the movies. Before the main film, audiences watched newsreels and short cartoons. The biggest cartoon star of the silent era was Felix the Cat, a black cat created at Pat Sullivan's studio in New York, with much of the animation by Otto Messmer, starting in 1919. Felix paced back and forth when he was thinking, and he could pull his tail off and use it as a cane or a question mark.

Meanwhile, in Kansas City and then in Los Angeles, a young cartoonist named Walt Disney was trying to build a studio. His closest partner was Ub Iwerks, a superb and very fast animator Disney had met in 1919, when both were young artists at a commercial art studio in Kansas City. In 1927 they created Oswald the Lucky Rabbit for Universal Pictures. Oswald was a hit, but in early 1928 Disney discovered that his distributor, Charles Mintz, and Universal owned the rights to Oswald, and that Mintz had hired away most of his animators. Disney lost his character and most of his team in one meeting.

Disney and Iwerks needed a new star, fast. Together they came up with a cheerful mouse. Iwerks did most of the drawing of the first films, and Walt Disney gave the character his personality and, soon, his voice. Mickey Mouse first appeared in a silent short called Plane Crazy, tested in front of an audience in May 1928, and then in another silent film, The Gallopin' Gaucho. Neither one found a distributor.

Then Disney had a bold idea. The Jazz Singer had just shown that audiences went wild for synchronized sound. What if a cartoon could have music and sound effects that matched the action exactly, so every footstep, whistle and honk landed on the beat? The third Mickey film, Steamboat Willie, was designed from the start for sound. The animators planned the action around a steady musical tempo, so they knew exactly which frame each beat would fall on. In a test screening in July 1928, Iwerks and others stood behind a bedsheet screen, banging pots and pans and blowing whistles in time with the picture, while Disney's family and staff watched to see if the sound felt real. It did.

Recording the real soundtrack was hard. The first recording session in New York, in September 1928, failed because the orchestra could not stay in time with the film. For the second attempt, the team used a click track, a steady clicking beat in the musicians' ears, and a filmed bouncing ball to help them follow the tempo. Disney, short of money, sold his car to help pay for it. The sound was recorded with Cinephone, a system belonging to the businessman Pat Powers that was based on Lee de Forest's sound-on-film technology.

Steamboat Willie opened on 18 November 1928 at the Colony Theatre in New York. Mickey steers a riverboat, whistling a tune, and later plays music on everything in sight: he cranks a goat's tail to make its mouth play like a music box, and uses a cow's teeth like a xylophone. Walt Disney himself provided Mickey's squeaks and laughs. Audiences loved it, and Mickey became a star almost overnight.

It is important to be fair about the history here. Steamboat Willie was not the first sound cartoon. The Fleischer brothers had made sing-along cartoons with a bouncing ball, the Song Car-Tunes, and some of these had sound from the mid-1920s using de Forest's Phonofilm. Another studio released a sound cartoon called Dinner Time a couple of months before Steamboat Willie. It was also not the first Mickey cartoon made; it was the third. What made it special was how tightly the music and action were tied together, and how much fun the result was. Steamboat Willie entered the public domain in the United States on 1 January 2024, meaning anyone can now share that first version of Mickey freely, although later versions of the character are still protected.

sections.heading: Shadow Puppets and the First Feature-Length Cartoons
paragraphs: Who made the first full-length animated movie? Many people would guess Disney, but the answer takes us to Argentina and Germany.

On 9 November 1917, a cinema in Buenos Aires showed El Apóstol (The Apostle), a political comedy made by the Italian-born cartoonist Quirino Cristiani for the producer Federico Valle. In the film, Argentina's president, Hipólito Yrigoyen, dreams of flying to Mount Olympus and borrowing thunderbolts from the god Zeus to blast corruption out of Buenos Aires. It ran about an hour and ten minutes and used tens of thousands of frames, many made with cutout figures moved by hand under the camera. El Apóstol is usually counted as the world's first animated feature film. Sadly, no one can watch it today: the only known copy was destroyed in a fire at Valle's studio in 1926. Cristiani made another feature, and later a sound feature, but those are lost too.

That makes our next film the oldest animated feature that still survives. In Berlin, a young woman named Lotte Reiniger had loved cutting paper silhouettes since childhood. She could snip a delicate figure, with lacy hair and curling fingers, out of black card in minutes. Reiniger built her characters from cardboard and thin sheets of lead, cutting each arm, leg and head separately and joining them with tiny wire hinges so the joints could bend. She laid the figures on a glass table lit from below, so they appeared as pure black shadows against glowing backgrounds, and moved them a fraction for each frame.

From 1923 to 1926, Reiniger worked on The Adventures of Prince Achmed, a tale inspired by the Arabian Nights, with a flying horse, an evil sorcerer, a witch, demons, and Aladdin with his magic lamp. Her husband, Carl Koch, ran the camera, and the experimental artists Walter Ruttmann and Berthold Bartosch helped create magical backgrounds and effects. Koch and Reiniger set up their camera above several layers of glass, so different parts of the scene could sit at different levels, an early relative of the multiplane camera that Disney would later make famous. The film premiered in Germany in September 1926 and runs a little over an hour.

The original prints were tinted in rich colors, so a scene might glow amber, deep blue or green. For many years only black-and-white copies were easy to see, but archivists in Germany and Britain restored the tinting in the late 1990s using surviving nitrate prints. Reiniger kept making silhouette films for the rest of her long life, and she is remembered as one of the great pioneers of animation, a woman director at a time when there were very few.

sections.heading: Giants One Frame at a Time: Stop-Motion
paragraphs: Animation does not have to be drawn. If you take a toy, photograph it, move it a tiny bit, and photograph it again, then play the pictures back quickly, the toy seems to come alive on its own. This is stop-motion animation, and it works with models, clay, puppets, even everyday objects. Early filmmakers such as the Russian-Polish animator Władysław Starewicz made remarkable stop-motion films in the 1910s using real beetles and other insects fitted with wire legs.

The great American pioneer was Willis H. O'Brien. He started by building small clay dinosaurs, and in 1915 he made The Dinosaur and the Missing Link, a short comedy, after an exhibitor saw about 90 seconds of his test footage and paid him to finish it. O'Brien's big break came with the 1925 film The Lost World, based on Arthur Conan Doyle's novel about explorers who find dinosaurs living on a remote plateau. Its dinosaurs had metal skeletons called armatures, with joints that could be bent and would stay put, covered in rubber skin. Some even had air bladders inside so their chests seemed to breathe.

Then came King Kong, which premiered in New York on 2 March 1933 at two huge theaters, Radio City Music Hall and the RKO Roxy. It was directed by Merian C. Cooper and Ernest B. Schoedsack, and O'Brien led the effects team. On screen, Kong looks like a monster tall enough to climb the Empire State Building. In reality, the main Kong models were only about 14 to 18 inches (36 to 46 centimeters) tall, built by the model-maker Marcel Delgado on metal armatures padded with cotton and latex and covered with rabbit fur.

Every time an animator touched Kong to move him for the next frame, the fur got pressed in slightly different directions. On screen, this makes Kong's fur ripple and shimmer, as if wind were blowing through it. It was an accident, but many viewers thought it made him seem more alive. For close-ups, the team also built a giant mechanical head and shoulders, operated from inside by several people, and a huge hand that could hold the actress Fay Wray.

The real magic was in combining things. O'Brien's team placed tiny model jungles in front of layered glass paintings to create depth. They used rear projection, shining a film onto a screen behind the actors, so Fay Wray could react to a dinosaur fight that was really happening on a screen behind her. They even built miniature rear-projection screens into the model sets, so a tiny moving image of a real actor appeared among the models. The stop-motion animation alone took about 55 weeks, and the animators had to keep the lighting exactly the same from one frame to the next, because even a small change would show up as flicker on screen.

sections.heading: Disney's Folly: Depth, Color and Snow White
paragraphs: After Mickey's success, the Disney studio kept experimenting. Its Silly Symphonies series let animators try new ideas set to music. In 1932 Flowers and Trees became the first cartoon made in full three-color Technicolor, and it won the very first Academy Award for an animated short. The Three Little Pigs in 1933 showed that cartoon characters could have truly different personalities, even when they looked alike. But Walt Disney dreamed of something much bigger: a cartoon as long as a regular feature film, one that could make people laugh, feel scared and even cry.

Many people in Hollywood thought this was a terrible idea. Who would sit through an 80-minute cartoon? Some called the project Disney's Folly. Disney chose the fairy tale Snow White, and work on it lasted several years, from the mid-1930s until the end of 1937. Hundreds of artists worked on it. Live-action reference films were shot of a young dancer, Marge Champion (then Marjorie Belcher), performing Snow White's movements, so animators could study how a real person walks, turns and dances. A young trained singer, Adriana Caselotti, gave Snow White her high, sweet voice.

One big problem was depth. When a cartoon camera moves toward a flat drawing, everything gets bigger at the same rate, like zooming into a photo. That looks flat and fake. In real life, when you walk through a forest, nearby trees slide past quickly while faraway mountains barely move. To capture this, Disney's engineer William Garity built the multiplane camera, completed in early 1937. It was a tall machine with a camera at the top pointing down through as many as seven layers of artwork painted on glass, each layer at a different distance and each able to move separately. Foreground branches could slide past fast, the middle of the scene a little slower, and the distant background slowest of all, just as in real vision.

Disney tested the multiplane camera on a short called The Old Mill (1937), in which a windmill and its animals ride out a thunderstorm. It won an Academy Award. Then the camera was put to work on Snow White, giving its forests and cottage a feeling of real depth. Ub Iwerks, who had left Disney for a while, had built his own multiplane device in 1933, and Lotte Reiniger had used layered glass years earlier, but Disney's version was the most advanced.

The cost kept climbing until it reached about 1.5 million dollars, a huge amount for the time. Disney had to borrow money from the Bank of America, and he had to show the bankers an unfinished version of the film to persuade them. Finally, on 21 December 1937, Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs premiered at the Carthay Circle Theatre in Los Angeles, with many Hollywood stars in the audience. Reports from the night say some of them cried when Snow White seemed to have died.

Snow White was the first full-length cel-animated feature in color with synchronized sound made in the United States, but remember that it was not the first animated feature ever. It became the highest-earning film of 1938, and Disney received a special Academy Award: one full-sized Oscar statuette and seven little ones, one for each dwarf, presented by the child star Shirley Temple. Songs like Heigh-Ho and Someday My Prince Will Come became classics. The Folly paid for Disney's new studio in Burbank.

Other studios followed. The Fleischers released their own feature, Gulliver's Travels, in December 1939, and in 1940 Disney released Pinocchio and Fantasia, which paired animation with classical music played by an orchestra conducted by Leopold Stokowski. In less than 50 years, moving drawings had gone from Reynaud hand-cranking painted squares in a wax museum to hundreds of artists building whole worlds of color, sound and depth.

Yet all this magic still belonged to big studios with giant cameras, painted glass and armies of artists. Outside the cinema, something just as important was happening in ordinary homes, schools and streets. Cameras were getting smaller, cheaper and easier. Soon a schoolteacher, a reporter, a farmer or a child would be able to carry a camera everywhere and catch real life as it happened. The 20th century was about to put a camera into almost everyone's hands.

deepDive: Who deserves the title of first animated film? It depends on how you define animation and film. Émile Reynaud's Théâtre Optique (1892) projected hand-painted moving images to paying audiences, but it used no camera and no photographic film, so some historians put it in a separate category of pre-cinema projection. J. Stuart Blackton's Humorous Phases of Funny Faces (1906) is often called the first animated cartoon on standard film, yet much of it is cutout animation rather than new drawings for each frame. Émile Cohl's Fantasmagorie (1908) is frequently named the first fully hand-drawn animated film, because nearly every frame is a new drawing. Even earlier, a few short experiments, such as some made for toy projectors in Germany, may qualify, and their exact dates are debated. The honest answer is that animation grew from many people's experiments at almost the same time. The arithmetic of animation explains why studios became factories. At 24 frames per second, one minute of film needs 1,440 frames. Animated on twos, that is still 720 drawings per minute, and an 80-minute feature needs over 57,000 drawings for a single character, before counting extra layers for other characters, effects like rain, and the many rough sketches that were thrown away. That is why the cel system, with backgrounds painted once and characters split across separate sheets, was such a big economic invention, and why the cel patents of Earl Hurd and his business partner, the studio owner John Randolph Bray, mattered so much in the 1910s and 1920s. Historians also discuss the hidden workforce. Disney's Ink and Paint department employed many women who mixed custom paints and traced animators' lines with great precision, yet animators, almost all men at the time, received most of the credit. Similarly, Ub Iwerks is now recognized as doing much of the drawing that created Mickey's first films, even though Walt Disney became the public face. Finally, there is the question of firsts in sound: the Fleischers' Song Car-Tunes and Dinner Time came before Steamboat Willie, but Steamboat Willie's careful planning of music and action on a frame-by-frame beat set the model for the cartoon soundtracks that followed.
funFact: King Kong, the giant ape who climbs the Empire State Building, was mostly played by models only about 14 to 18 inches (36 to 46 centimeters) tall, covered in rabbit fur.

check.q: Why was Steamboat Willie (1928) so famous, even though it was not the first sound cartoon?
check.a: Its music and sound effects were tightly synchronized with the action
wrong: It was the first cartoon ever made
It was the first cartoon in full color
It was the first feature-length cartoon
